Chapter overview

Modern Tamil literature moves from nineteenth-century printing and literary revival through manuscript scholarship, renaissance movements, poetry, prose, novels, short stories, theatre, journals and modern reference research.

Print transitionRenaissanceCreative genresJournalsScholarship
Period, Printing and the Nineteenth-Century Transition

Modern Tamil literature emerged through printing, education, reform, prose and the formation of a new reading public.

Period and Scope

Modern Tamil literature broadly developed from the nineteenth century to the later decades of the twentieth century.

This chapter covers:

  • Tamil literary renaissance
  • Recovery and publication of ancient manuscripts
  • Growth of printing and journalism
  • Modern poetry
  • Modern prose and essays
  • Tamil novels
  • Short stories
  • Modern drama
  • Important literary journals
  • Major author–work associations

Writers and movements mainly belonging to the post-1970 period are covered in Chapter 8: Contemporary Tamil Literature.

Chapter 7 focuses on printing, literary firsts and the formation of modern genres. For writers whose careers continue after Independence, only their role in genre development is noted here; their mature works, later movements and post-Independence significance are studied in Chapter 8.

Growth of Printing

Printing accelerated the development of:

  • Prose writing
  • Newspapers
  • Periodicals
  • Textbooks
  • Dictionaries
  • Translations
  • Novels
  • Short stories
  • Modern drama
  • Publication of palm-leaf manuscripts

Printing enabled ancient Tamil works to circulate beyond traditional scholars and manuscript libraries.

Missionaries, Tamil scholars, editors and publishers contributed to the growth of modern Tamil prose.

Missionary presses, Tamil-owned presses and educational institutions expanded the production of religious books, school texts, dictionaries, translations and literary works.

Western education, social and religious reform, newspapers and journals created a new reading public beyond traditional manuscript circles.

Navalar, Meenakshisundaram Pillai and Early Literary Revival

Early revival combined Saiva printing, traditional literary teaching, Vallalar’s ethics and music-centred public literature.

Arumuga Navalar

Birthplace: Nallur, Jaffna

Period: 1822–1879

Arumuga Navalar contributed to:

  • Tamil prose
  • Saiva education
  • Textbook production
  • Printing
  • Editing Saiva works
  • Publication of classical texts

He established printing presses and schools in Jaffna and Tamil Nadu.

His prose was direct, instructional and suited to school education and religious explanation.

Mahavidwan Meenakshisundaram Pillai

Period: 1815–1876

Title: Mahavidwan

Other description: Modern Kambar

Associated institution: Tiruvavaduthurai Adheenam

He composed:

  • Sthalapuranas
  • Pillaittamil works
  • Antatis
  • Kalambakams
  • Ulas
  • Individual poems

He was the principal Tamil teacher of U. V. Swaminatha Iyer.

Tamil Virtual Academy records that he composed approximately 61 works.

Ramalinga Adigal

Other names: Vallalar and Arutprakasa Vallalar

Birthplace: Marudhur near Chidambaram

Period: 1823–1874

Important works include:

  • Thiruvarutpa
  • Manumurai Kanda Vasagam
  • Jeevakarunya Ozhukkam
  • Arutperunjothi Agaval

Thiruvarutpa was arranged into six Thirumurais.

Important literary themes include:

  • Compassion towards all living beings
  • Opposition to hunger
  • Spiritual light
  • Religious harmony
  • Jeevakarunyam

Vallalar’s prose contributed to the development of lucid nineteenth-century Tamil writing.

Vallalar founded the Samarasa Suddha Sanmarga Sangam and made compassion, feeding the hungry and Jeevakarunyam central to his literary and spiritual message.

Gopalakrishna Bharati

Period: Nineteenth century

Major work: Nandanar Charitra Keerthanai

Nandanar Charitra Keerthanai narrates the life of Nandanar, one of the 63 Nayanmars.

The work combines:

  • Story
  • Music
  • Dialogue
  • Keerthanai form
  • Social observations

It became highly influential in Tamil music, theatre and later performance traditions.

Annamalai Reddiar

Period: 1865–1891

Major work: Kavadi Chindu

Annamalai Reddiar is popularly called:

  • Kavadi Chindu Annamalai Reddiar
  • Father of Kavadi Chindu

Kavadi Chindu combines:

  • Folk rhythm
  • Murugan devotion
  • Simple Tamil
  • Musical performance

His compositions strongly influenced stage drama and Tamil music.

Musical Poetry and Bharati

Subramania Bharati’s songs combined literary innovation with rhythms suited to public singing, nationalist mobilisation, children’s education and devotional performance.

Damodaram Pillai and U. V. Swaminatha Iyer

Damodaram Pillai and U. V. Swaminatha Iyer preserved classical Tamil through distinct but complementary editorial methods.

C. W. Damodaram Pillai

Full name: C. Vai. Damodaram Pillai

Period: 1832–1901

He collected, edited and printed ancient Tamil works from palm-leaf manuscripts.

Important works associated with his editorial activity include:

  • Tolkappiyam
  • Kalithokai
  • Virasoliyam
  • Ilakkanavilakkam
  • Sulamani

He was one of the earliest scholars to use printed critical editions to preserve ancient Tamil texts.

Damodaram Pillai’s work preceded and complemented the manuscript-publication work of U. V. Swaminatha Iyer.

His editorial activity also helped preserve Iraiyanar Akapporul and strengthened the early print-based recovery of Tamil grammar and classical literature.

U. V. Swaminatha Iyer

Period: 1855–1942

Birthplace: Uthamadhanapuram

Popular title: Tamil Thatha

Teacher: Mahavidwan Meenakshisundaram Pillai

U. V. Swaminatha Iyer travelled throughout Tamil regions to collect palm-leaf manuscripts.

He:

  • Compared different manuscript copies
  • Corrected damaged passages
  • Added introductions and notes
  • Identified authors and commentaries
  • Published rare classical works

Important publications include:

  • Civaka Cintamani — 1887
  • Pattuppattu — 1889
  • Silappadikaram — 1892
  • Purananuru — 1894
  • Manimekalai — 1898
  • Perunkathai — 1924

His autobiography is En Charithiram.

His wider manuscript work also supported the recovery and circulation of Pathitrupathu and Ainkurunuru.

Damodaram Pillai was an earlier pioneer of critical printed editions, while U. V. Swaminatha Iyer undertook extensive field collection, manuscript comparison, annotation and publication across a wider classical corpus.

Tamil Renaissance and the Pure Tamil Movement

The Tamil Renaissance and Pure Tamil Movement strengthened language identity, antiquity studies and Tamil-centred vocabulary.

Tamil Renaissance

The Tamil Renaissance strengthened interest in Tamil antiquity, classical literature, linguistic identity, inscriptions, literary history and Dravidian language studies.

It developed through scholarship, institutions, journals, language research and public campaigns for Tamil in education and cultural life.

Robert Caldwell

Robert Caldwell’s comparative study helped establish the Dravidian languages as a distinct language family and influenced modern discussions of Tamil linguistic identity.

G. U. Pope

G. U. Pope translated and interpreted major Tamil classics, including Thirukkural and Tiruvacakam, for an international readership.

Pandithurai Thevar

Period: 1867–1911

Institution: Fourth Tamil Sangam, Madurai

Year established: 1901

Pandithurai Thevar founded the modern Madurai Tamil Sangam.

The institution supported:

  • Tamil research
  • Manuscript publication
  • Literary conferences
  • Tamil examinations
  • Scholars and poets

Its journal was called Senthamizh.

The institution was popularly described as the Fourth Tamil Sangam.

Parithimar Kalaignar

Original name: V. G. Suryanarayana Sastri

Period: 1870–1903

Birthplace: Vilacheri near Madurai

Institution: Madras Christian College

He changed his Sanskrit-derived name to the Tamil name Parithimar Kalaignar.

Important works include:

  • Tamil Mozhiyin Varalaru
  • Nadagaviyal
  • Kalavathi
  • Rupavathi
  • Maanavijayam
  • Tamil Viyasangal

He argued that Tamil was an independent classical language and opposed attempts to remove Tamil from higher education.

His article Uyarthani Semmozhi was published in the Senthamizh journal in the early twentieth century.

Maraimalai Adigal

Original name: Vedachalam

Period: 1876–1950

Title: Father of the Pure Tamil Movement

He formally promoted the Tanittamil Iyakkam from 1916.

Important prose works include:

  • Arivurai Kothu
  • Velalar Nagarigam
  • Siruvarkkana Sentamil
  • Makkal Nootrandu Uyir Vazhkkai
  • Kokilambal Kadithangal

Kokilambal Kadithangal is an epistolary novel.

Maraimalai Adigal promoted writing that avoided Sanskrit loanwords and preferred Tamil equivalents.

Devaneya Pavanar

Devaneya Pavanar was associated with Pure Tamil scholarship, Tamil etymology and arguments concerning the antiquity and independent development of Tamil.

Subramania Bharati: Poetry, Prose and Journalism

Bharati transformed poetry, prose and journalism through nationalism, equality, freedom and literary innovation.

Subramania Bharati

Period: 1882–1921

Birthplace: Ettayapuram

Popular titles: Mahakavi and Desiya Kavi

Original name: Subramanian

The Ettayapuram court gave him the title Bharati when he was about eleven years old.

Bharati modernised Tamil poetry through:

  • Simple and energetic language
  • New rhythms
  • Nationalist poetry
  • Women’s liberation
  • Social equality
  • Children’s poetry
  • Devotional poetry
  • Prose poetry
  • Journalism

He used both traditional metres and innovative poetic forms.

Bharati’s Major Works
National and Social Poetry
  • Sudesa Geethangal
  • Janmabhoomi
  • Viduthalai songs
  • Puthiya Aathichudi
  • Pappa Pattu
Long Poems
  • Panchali Sabatham
  • Kuyil Pattu
  • Kannan Pattu
Prose and Fiction
  • Gnana Ratham
  • Chandrikaiyin Kathai
  • Chinna Sankaran Kathai
  • Aaril Oru Pangu
  • Irul

Panchali Sabatham uses Draupadi and the Mahabharata narrative to represent national humiliation and resistance.

Kannan Pattu presents Krishna through several relationships, including child, friend, lover and deity.

Kuyil Pattu is a philosophical and imaginative poem.

Bharati and Journalism

Bharati worked with or contributed to journals including:

  • Swadesamitran
  • India
  • Vijaya
  • Chakravarthini
  • Bala Bharata

His journalistic prose was:

  • Direct
  • Energetic
  • Satirical
  • Political
  • Accessible to ordinary readers

Detailed information on his role in the freedom struggle belongs to Chapter 17.

Bharathidasan and Major Modern Poets

Bharathidasan and other modern poets widened Tamil poetry through social equality, regional identity, popular song and modern imagery.

Bharathidasan

Original name: Kanakasabai Subburathinam

Period: 1891–1964

Birthplace: Puducherry

Titles: Pavendar and Puratchi Kavignar

He adopted the name Bharathidasan because of his admiration for Subramania Bharati.

His poetry focused on:

  • Tamil language
  • Social equality
  • Women’s education
  • Labourers
  • Opposition to caste
  • Rational thought
  • Nature
  • Family welfare

The detailed connection between Bharathidasan and socio-political movements belongs to Chapters 23–27.

Bharathidasan’s Major Works
Poetry and Narrative Works
  • Pandiyan Parisu
  • Ethirparatha Mutham
  • Kudumba Vilakku
  • Irunda Veedu
  • Azhagin Sirippu
  • Tamil Iyakkam
  • Isai Amuthu
  • Kuyil
  • Tamilachiyin Kathi
  • Kurinjithittu
  • Bharathidasan Aathichudi
Drama
  • Pisirandaiyar
  • Amaithi–Oomai

Bharathidasan received the Sahitya Akademi Award posthumously in 1970 for the drama Pisirandaiyar.

Kavimani Desigavinayagam Pillai

Period: 1876–1954

Title: Kavimani

Important works include:

  • Malarum Malaiyum
  • Nanjil Nattu Marumakkal Vazhi Manmiyam
  • Asia Jothi
  • Umar Khayyam songs

His poetry is known for:

  • Simplicity
  • Children’s songs
  • Devotional themes
  • Social observation
  • Translations and adaptations
Namakkal Kavignar

Full name: V. Ramalingam Pillai

Period: 1888–1972

Title: Namakkal Kavignar

His famous nationalist line begins:

Kathiyindri Raththamindri Yuththam Ondru Varuguthu

Important works include:

  • Malaikallan
  • En Kathai
  • Avanum Avalum
  • Sangoli

His poems promoted nationalism, Gandhian ideals and Tamil identity.

Pattukottai Kalyanasundaram

Period: 1930–1959

Popular title: Makkal Kavignar

He became famous through Tamil film songs.

His songs dealt with:

  • Labour
  • Social inequality
  • Self-respect
  • Political awareness
  • Rural life
  • Hope and progress

His simple vocabulary and folk rhythms brought socially oriented poetry to a mass audience.

Kannadasan

Original name: Muthiah

Period: 1927–1981

Title: Kaviyarasu

Important works include:

  • Arthamulla Hindu Matham
  • Yesu Kaviyam
  • Cheraman Kathali
  • Vanavasam
  • Manavasam

He also wrote numerous poems, essays, novels and film lyrics.

His detailed contribution extends into the contemporary period and may also be studied with Chapter 8.

Suddhananda Bharati

Suddhananda Bharati wrote nationalist, spiritual and reform-oriented poetry and used Tamil as a vehicle for freedom, human unity and cultural renewal.

Suratha

Suratha became known for image-rich modern poetry and was popularly associated with the title Uvamai Kavignar, or poet of similes.

Abdul Rahman

Abdul Rahman, popularly called Kavikko, brought modern imagery, philosophical reflection and accessible free-verse expression into Tamil poetry.

Modern Tamil Prose and Thiru. Vi. Ka.

Modern prose grew through essays, biographies, reform writing, journalism and accessible public language.

Development of Prose

Modern Tamil prose expanded through:

  • Religious publications
  • Textbooks
  • Newspapers
  • Essays
  • Political writing
  • Biographies
  • Autobiographies
  • Travel writing
  • Novels
  • Short stories

Important prose writers included:

  • Mayuram Vedanayagam Pillai
  • U. V. Swaminatha Iyer
  • Subramania Bharati
  • Thiru. Vi. Kalyanasundaranar
  • Maraimalai Adigal
  • Pudhumaipithan

Tamil Virtual Academy identifies Bharati, Pudhumaipithan, Thiru. Vi. Ka. and Maraimalai Adigal as important twentieth-century prose writers.

Thiru. Vi. Kalyanasundaranar

Popular name: Thiru. Vi. Ka.

Title: Tamil Thendral

Period: 1883–1953

Important prose works include:

  • Pennin Perumai
  • Murugan Allathu Azhagu
  • Manitha Vazhkkaiyum Gandhiyadigalum
  • En Kadan Pani Seythu Kidappathe
  • Kathiraiver Pillai Charithiram

He edited journals including:

  • Desabhaktan
  • Navasakthi

His prose combined literary Tamil with an effective public-speaking style.

Detailed political and labour activities belong to later socio-political chapters.

He was also a labour leader whose journalism and public prose connected Tamil scholarship with social and political mobilisation.

The First Tamil Novels

The first Tamil novels established prose fiction through adventure, domestic philosophy and social reform.

Prathapa Mudaliar Charithram

Author: Mayuram Vedanayagam Pillai

Published: 1879

Status: First published Tamil novel

The novel follows the adventures of Prathapa Mudaliar and Gnanambal.

It contains:

  • Adventure
  • Humour
  • Folk-tale elements
  • Social observations
  • Prose narrative

Vedanayagam Pillai also wrote Suguna Sundari.

Prathapa Mudaliar Charithram marked the beginning of the Tamil novel as a distinct literary form.

Kamalambal Charithram

Author: B. R. Rajam Iyer

Serial publication: Viveka Chintamani

Period: 1890s

Earlier title: Aabathukkidamana Apavadham

The novel examines:

  • Family relationships
  • Rural and urban life
  • Religious and philosophical questions
  • Social customs
  • Spiritual transformation

It is regarded as one of the earliest artistically structured Tamil novels and an early Tamil serial novel.

Padmavathi Charithram

Author: A. Madhaviah

Period: Late nineteenth century

The novel discusses:

  • Child marriage
  • Widowhood
  • Women’s education
  • Family customs
  • Social reform

Madhaviah used realistic prose to expose problems affecting women in contemporary society.

His other works include:

  • Muthu Meenakshi
  • Clarinda
  • Kusikar Kutti Kathaigal
Major Modern Novelists and Historical Fiction

Historical fiction and major modern novelists expanded the reading public through magazines, serialisation and diverse social themes.

Kalki R. Krishnamurthy

Period: 1899–1954

Pen name: Kalki

Fields: Novel, short story, essay, criticism and journalism

Historical Novels
  • Parthiban Kanavu — Pallava period
  • Sivagamiyin Sabatham — Pallava–Chalukya conflict
  • Ponniyin Selvan — early life of Arulmozhi Varman
Social and Political Novels
  • Kalvanin Kadhali
  • Thyaga Bhoomi
  • Alai Osai

Ponniyin Selvan was serialised in the Kalki magazine between 1950 and 1954.

Kalki combined historical research, suspense, romance and serial narration.

Akilan

Akilan wrote historical and social novels. Vengayin Maindhan is associated with Chola history, while Chithira Pavai received the Jnanpith Award.

Sandilyan

Sandilyan popularised maritime and historical adventure fiction through novels such as Kadal Pura and Yavana Rani.

Na. Parthasarathy

Na. Parthasarathy wrote novels including Kurinji Malar and was closely associated with the literary journal Deepam.

V. M. Kothainayaki Ammal

Period: 1901–1960

Role: Novelist, editor and public speaker

Journal: Jaganmohini

She was one of the leading early women novelists in Tamil.

Her writings dealt with:

  • Women’s education
  • Family life
  • Nationalism
  • Social responsibility
  • Women’s public participation

She wrote numerous novels and encouraged women readers and writers through Jaganmohini.

Other Women Novelists
Lakshmi

Lakshmi was an important woman novelist associated with family life, women’s experience and social relationships.

Rajam Krishnan

Rajam Krishnan combined social research with fiction on women, workers, rural communities and marginalised occupations.

Anuthama

Anuthama contributed to family-centred and socially observant Tamil fiction.

Sivasankari

Sivasankari wrote socially engaged novels on family relationships, migration, alcoholism and women’s lives.

Indumathi

Indumathi contributed to popular modern Tamil fiction with attention to relationships and changing urban society.

Origins of the Modern Tamil Short Story

The modern short story emerged from print culture, concise narration and new realist and psychological techniques.

Transition to the Modern Short Story

The modern Tamil short story developed from oral tales and prose narratives under the influence of print periodicals and new compact fictional forms.

Its structure differed from traditional tales through concentration, unity of effect, realistic characterisation and concise narration.

Early Short-Story Writers

The early development of the modern Tamil short story is associated with:

  • A. Madhaviah
  • Subramania Bharati
  • V. V. S. Aiyar

Madhaviah’s Kusikar Kutti Kathaigal was first written in English and later translated into Tamil.

Bharati wrote stories including Aaril Oru Pangu and Irul.

Kulathangarai Arasamaram

Author: V. V. S. Aiyar

Published in collection: Mangaiyarkarasiyin Kadhal Mudaliya Kathaigal

Year of collection: 1912

Kulathangarai Arasamaram dealt with the dowry problem.

Several literary historians regard it as the first fully developed modern Tamil short story.

The claim is not completely uncontested because earlier prose narratives and stories also existed.

Manikkodi and Pudhumaipithan

Manikkodi and Pudhumaipithan made experimentation, satire, criticism and social realism central to modern short fiction.

Manikkodi Era

The period from approximately 1926 to 1945 is often described as a golden age of the Tamil short story.

The journal Manikkodi encouraged experimentation in:

  • Language
  • Narrative structure
  • Psychological writing
  • Social criticism
  • Satire
  • Symbolism

Important Manikkodi-era writers included:

  • Pudhumaipithan
  • Ku. Pa. Rajagopalan
  • Na. Pichamurthy
  • Mouni
  • B. S. Ramaiah

Kalaimagal and Ananda Vikatan also encouraged short-story writing.

Manikkodi emerged in the 1930s as a major platform for modernist short fiction, criticism and experiments in language and narrative form.

Chitti and C. S. Chellappa were also associated with the wider Manikkodi literary environment.

Pudhumaipithan

Original name: C. Viruthachalam

Period: 1906–1948

Pen name: Pudhumaipithan

Important stories include:

  • Ponnagaram
  • Saapa Vimochanam
  • Kadavulum Kandasami Pillaiyum
  • Kalyani
  • Kayittraravu

His stories used:

  • Social satire
  • Irony
  • Realism
  • Mythological reinterpretation
  • Criticism of poverty and hypocrisy
  • Psychological conflict

Ponnagaram examines poverty and the social idea of chastity.

Saapa Vimochanam reinterprets the Ahalya narrative.

Other Major Short-Story Writers

Later short-story writers developed psychological, rural, regional, urban, feminist and experimental traditions.

Other Important Short-Story Writers
Ku. Pa. Rajagopalan

Known for sensitive treatment of family relationships and human emotions.

Na. Pichamurthy

Associated with psychological fiction and later free-verse experimentation.

Mouni

Known for symbolism, silence and internal psychological conflict.

B. S. Ramaiah

Writer and important figure associated with Manikkodi.

La. Sa. Ramamirtham

Known for distinctive prose rhythm and exploration of family memory.

T. Janakiraman

Known for refined prose, music, relationships and middle-class life.

Ku. Alagirisamy

Known for rural settings and realistic characterisation.

Writers such as Jayakanthan, Ashokamitran, Sundara Ramasamy and Indira Parthasarathy form an important bridge to contemporary Tamil literature and are covered more fully in Chapter 8.

Later Major Short-Story Voices
Jayakanthan

Jayakanthan used social realism to portray urban poverty, marginal lives, relationships and moral conflict.

Ki. Rajanarayanan

Ki. Rajanarayanan brought Karisal regional speech, oral storytelling and rural social memory into modern fiction.

Ashokamitran

Ashokamitran portrayed Chennai’s middle-class life, cinema workers, urban isolation and ordinary experience through restrained prose.

Sujatha

Sujatha expanded short fiction through science, technology, urban life, suspense and highly readable modern prose.

Vannadasan

Vannadasan is known for subtle short stories centred on ordinary people, everyday emotion and close observation.

Prapanchan

Prapanchan wrote social and historical fiction, often drawing on Puducherry and colonial experience.

Ambai

Ambai’s stories foreground women’s bodies, domestic labour, travel, music, memory and independence.

Modern Tamil Drama

Modern Tamil drama developed from company theatre into reformed prose drama and social-political performance.

Beginning of Modern Drama

The year 1870 is commonly treated as a starting point for modern Tamil drama.

Modern Tamil theatre developed under the influence of:

  • Traditional Koothu
  • Musical drama
  • Parsi theatre
  • English theatre
  • Shakespearean drama
  • Professional drama companies

Sankaradas Swamigal, Pammal Sambandha Mudaliar and Parithimar Kalaignar are described as the Trinity of Modern Tamil Drama.

Sankaradas Swamigal

Period: 1867–1922

Titles: Father of Tamil Theatre and Everest of Tamil Drama

He worked as:

  • Playwright
  • Actor
  • Director
  • Teacher
  • Drama-company organiser

Important plays include:

  • Valli Thirumanam
  • Pavalakodi
  • Sathi Anusuya
  • Abhimanyu Sundari
  • Kovalan Charithiram
  • Alli Arjuna

His Boys Company tradition trained several later Tamil stage performers.

His plays combined dialogue, songs, mythology and popular performance.

Pammal Sambandha Mudaliar

Period: 1873–1964

Popular title: Father of Modern Tamil Drama

Associated organisation: Suguna Vilasa Sabha

Important plays include:

  • Manohara
  • Sabapathi
  • Pushpavalli
  • Ratnavali
  • Kalvar Thalaivan

He:

  • Reduced excessive dependence on songs
  • Strengthened spoken dialogue
  • Improved stage direction
  • Introduced rehearsal discipline
  • Adapted Shakespearean plays
  • Promoted realistic acting

His work helped transform musical theatre into modern prose drama.

Parithimar Kalaignar and Drama

Important dramatic works include:

  • Kalavathi
  • Rupavathi
  • Maanavijayam

His Nadagaviyal deals with the principles and grammar of drama.

He wrote both prose and verse plays and personally performed female roles in some productions.

T. K. Shanmugam

T. K. Shanmugam was a major actor and theatre organiser associated with professional drama companies and celebrated stage productions such as Avvaiyar.

Social and Political Theatre
C. N. Annadurai

Annadurai used social and political drama in works such as Velaikkari and Or Iravu.

M. Karunanidhi

Karunanidhi used forceful dialogue and political themes in plays including Manimagudam.

Journals and the Modern Literary Public

Journals created a modern literary public through serialisation, criticism, debate and recurring writer–reader communities.

Importance of Journals

Journals supported the growth of:

  • Essays
  • Serial novels
  • Short stories
  • Poetry
  • Literary criticism
  • Political prose
  • Public debate

Important modern Tamil journals included:

  • Swadesamitran
  • India
  • Vijaya
  • Viveka Chintamani
  • Senthamizh
  • Gnana Bodhini
  • Ananda Vikatan
  • Kalaimagal
  • Manikkodi
  • Kalki
  • Jaganmohini

Manikkodi became especially influential in the development of experimental short fiction.

Journal–Editor and Literary Associations
Swadesamitran

Swadesamitran developed Tamil journalism and was associated with G. Subramania Iyer and later writers including Bharati.

India and Vijaya

India and Vijaya are closely associated with Bharati’s nationalist journalism.

Navasakthi

Navasakthi was edited by Thiru. Vi. Ka. and connected literary prose with public and labour issues.

Ananda Vikatan

Ananda Vikatan promoted humour, essays, serial fiction and short stories; Kalki worked in its editorial world before founding his own magazine.

Kalki

Kalki magazine became a major platform for serial fiction, including Ponniyin Selvan.

Manikkodi

Manikkodi was central to modernist short stories, criticism and literary experimentation.

Saraswati

Saraswati supported modern Tamil literary discussion, criticism and creative writing.

Ezhuthu

C. S. Chellappa founded Ezhuthu in 1959; it promoted free verse, criticism and modernist writing.

Deepam

Deepam was associated with Na. Parthasarathy and published fiction and literary criticism.

Kanaiyazhi

Kanaiyazhi became an important platform for modern short stories, poetry and criticism and was associated with writers including Ashokamitran and T. Janakiraman.

Reference Works and Modern Tamil Scholarship

Reference works and scholarship organised Tamil vocabulary, authors, texts, history and linguistic research.

Abithana Chintamani

Author: A. Singaravelu Mudaliar

Type: Encyclopaedic reference work

Abithana Chintamani provides information on:

  • Tamil literature
  • Authors
  • Religion
  • Mythology
  • Historical traditions
  • Literary terms

It became an important reference work for Tamil scholars and students.

Tamil Lexicon

The Tamil Lexicon was prepared by the University of Madras.

It drew vocabulary from:

  • Sangam literature
  • Medieval texts
  • Religious literature
  • Modern writing
  • Regional usage
  • Inscriptions
  • Dictionaries

Scholars such as S. Vaiyapuri Pillai played an important role in Tamil lexicography and literary research.

S. Vaiyapuri Pillai

Period: 1891–1956

Fields: Lexicography, literary history and textual research

Important works include:

  • Ilakkiya Deepam
  • Kamban Kaviyam
  • History of Tamil Language and Literature

He was closely associated with the preparation of the University of Madras Tamil Lexicon.

Mu. Raghava Iyengar

Period: 1878–1960

Fields: Tamil history, literature and epigraphy

Important works include:

  • Velir Varalaru
  • Cheran Senguttuvan
  • Alvargal Kalanilai
  • Sasana Tamil Kavi Charitham

His research helped connect Tamil literature with inscriptions and historical evidence.

Tamil Encyclopaedic and University Scholarship

Modern Tamil scholarship expanded through dictionaries, encyclopaedias, literary histories, textual editions, linguistic research and university-based Tamil studies.

Mu. Varadarajan

Mu. Varadarajan, widely known as Mu. Va., contributed to Tamil literary history, criticism, language studies and university teaching.

T. P. Meenakshisundaran

T. P. Meenakshisundaran contributed to Tamil linguistics, literary history and comparative language scholarship.

Mayilai Seeni Venkatasami

Mayilai Seeni Venkatasami connected Tamil literature with archaeology, religion, inscriptions, art and cultural history.

R. Raghava Iyengar

R. Raghava Iyengar contributed to classical Tamil research, literary criticism and the study of poets and texts.

K. A. Nilakanta Sastri

K. A. Nilakanta Sastri’s historical scholarship on South India and the Cholas provided an important context for interpreting Tamil political and cultural history.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

This final topic consolidates authors, works, journals, movements, literary firsts and high-yield distinctions.

Rapid Revision

  • Vallalar — Thiruvarutpa
  • Arumuga Navalar — prose, printing and Saiva publications
  • Meenakshisundaram Pillai — teacher of U. V. Swaminatha Iyer

High-Yield Distinctions
  • Prathapa Mudaliar Charithram is the first published Tamil novel.
  • Kamalambal Charithram is associated with B. R. Rajam Iyer, not Vedanayagam Pillai.
  • Padmavathi Charithram was written by A. Madhaviah.
  • Kulathangarai Arasamaram was written by V. V. S. Aiyar and is frequently identified as the first modern Tamil short story.
  • Manikkodi is associated primarily with modern short stories and literary experimentation.
  • Pudhumaipithan’s original name was C. Viruthachalam.
  • Bharathidasan’s original name was Kanaka Subburathinam.
  • Maraimalai Adigal is associated with the Pure Tamil Movement.
  • Parithimar Kalaignar argued for Tamil’s classical-language status.
  • Pandithurai Thevar founded the modern Madurai Tamil Sangam in 1901.
  • U. V. Swaminatha Iyer recovered and published classical works; he did not compose those ancient texts.
  • Sankaradas Swamigal strengthened professional musical theatre.
  • Pammal Sambandha Mudaliar promoted modern prose dialogue and realistic staging.
  • Panchali Sabatham was written by Bharati; Pisirandaiyar was written by Bharathidasan.
  • Ponniyin Selvan was written by Kalki and concerns the early life of Arulmozhi Varman.
  • Modern Tamil literature and contemporary Tamil literature overlap chronologically, but post-1970 literary movements and newer voices are treated separately in Chapter 8.
  • C. W. Damodaram Pillai pioneered early critical print editions; U. V. Swaminatha Iyer undertook extensive manuscript travel, comparison and annotated publication.
  • Tamil Renaissance revived classical, linguistic and historical interest; the Pure Tamil Movement specifically preferred Tamil vocabulary over Sanskrit loans.
  • Subramania Bharati combined nationalism, social reform, prose and journalism; Bharathidasan developed Tamil identity, equality and Dravidian-oriented social poetry.
  • Bharati’s poetry used lyric and narrative forms; his journalism used direct political prose in India, Vijaya and other periodicals.
  • Prathapa Mudaliar Charithram is the first published Tamil novel; Kamalambal Charithram is an early philosophical and domestic novel.
  • Kamalambal Charithram was written by B. R. Rajam Iyer; Padmavathi Charithram by A. Madhaviah.
  • Prathapa Mudaliar Charithram is the first published Tamil novel; Kulathangarai Arasamaram is frequently identified as the first fully developed modern Tamil short story.
  • Kalki combined historical research and serial narration; Sandilyan became especially known for maritime historical adventure.
  • Manikkodi was a journal; the Manikkodi movement refers to the wider modernist literary tendency associated with it.
  • Pudhumaipithan is noted for satire and social realism; Mouni for symbolism, silence and inner psychological conflict.
  • Sankaradas Swamigal strengthened musical company drama; Pammal Sambandha Mudaliar promoted prose dialogue, rehearsal discipline and realistic staging.
  • Ananda Vikatan promoted humour and popular serial writing; Kalki became strongly associated with historical serial fiction.
  • Tamil Lexicon is a University of Madras lexicographical project; Abithana Chintamani is an encyclopaedic reference work by A. Singaravelu Mudaliar.
  • Creative literature includes poetry, fiction and drama; reference scholarship includes lexicons, encyclopaedias, textual editions and literary histories.
